title_en: Supreme People's Court, Supreme People's Procuratorate, Ministry of Justice, and Ministry of Public Security — Standard for Identification of Grievous Bodily Harm
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court, Supreme People's Procuratorate, Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Public Security

Standards for Identification of Serious Injuries

Judicial [1990] No. 070

Chapter I General Provisions

Article 1 These Standards are formulated in accordance with the provisions of Article 85 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China, based on the theories and techniques of medicine and forensic medicine, and combined with the practical experience of forensic examination in China, to provide a scientific basis and uniform standards for the identification of serious injuries.

Article 2 "Serious injury" means an injury that causes disability of a limb, disfigurement of a person's appearance, loss of hearing, loss of vision, loss of function of other organs, or other serious harm to a person's health.

Article 3 When assessing the degree of injury, the principle of seeking truth from facts must be adhered to, and the specific injury circumstances must be analyzed concretely. The degree of injury includes the original pathological changes at the time of injury, complications directly related to the injury, and sequelae caused by the injury. When conducting an identification, a comprehensive analysis and overall assessment shall be made based on the injury at the time of injury and its consequences or outcomes.

Article 4 The identifier responsible for identifying the degree of injury shall be a forensic physician or a person qualified for forensic medical identification, or may be a physician at or above the level of attending doctor entrusted or appointed by judicial authorities. During identification, the identifier has the right to learn about the circumstances relevant to the injury, inspect case files and medical records, and examine the scene; the relevant units have the responsibility to cooperate. The identifier shall comply with relevant legal provisions and maintain the confidentiality of the case.

Article 5 The identification of the degree of injury shall be completed before the judgment is rendered.

Chapter II Disability of Limbs

Article 6 "Disability of limbs" means the loss of a limb or the loss of function of a limb although it remains intact due to various causative factors.

Article 7 "Loss of a limb" means any of the following circumstances:
(1) Loss of any thumb exceeding the interphalangeal joint;
(2) Loss of any three fingers other than the thumb of one hand exceeding the proximal interphalangeal joints, or loss of any four fingers other than the thumbs of both hands exceeding the proximal interphalangeal joints;
(3) Loss of any two fingers together with their connected metacarpal bones;
(4) Loss of fifty percent of one foot or fifty percent of the heel;
(5) Loss of the first toe of one foot and any other two toes, or loss of four toes of one foot other than the first toe;
(6) Loss of five or more toes of both feet;
(7) Loss of the first toe of any foot together with its connected metatarsal bone;
(8) Loss of any three toes of one foot other than the first toe together with their connected metatarsal bones.

Article 8 "Loss of function of a limb although it remains intact" means any of the following circumstances:
(1) Ankylosis or deformity of the shoulder joint with loss of up to fifty percent [1] of joint range of motion;
(2) Restriction of elbow joint movement in the extended position with a range of motion less than 90 degrees, or restriction in the functional position with a range of motion less than 10 degrees;
(3) Fracture of the humerus complicated by pseudoarthrosis or malunion severely affecting upper limb function;
(4) Malunion of forearm fracture with ankylosis in pronation or supination;
(5) Forearm fracture causing severe impairment of wrist, palm, or finger function;
(6) Soft tissue injury of the forearm causing severe impairment of wrist, palm, or finger function;
(7) Ankylosis, contracture deformity of the wrist joint, or loss of up to fifty percent of joint range of motion;
(8) Fracture of the metacarpal or phalangeal bones affecting hand function, with inability to oppose fingers and grasp objects [2];
(9) Contracture deformity of the thumb of one hand, with inability to oppose fingers and grasp objects;
(10) Contracture deformity of any three fingers other than the thumb of one hand, with inability to oppose fingers and grasp objects;
(11) Ankylosis, contracture deformity of the hip joint, or loss of up to fifty percent of joint range of motion;
(12) Ankylosis, contracture deformity of the knee joint with flexion exceeding 30 degrees, or loss of up to fifty percent of joint range of motion;
(13) Injury to the cruciate ligament of any knee causing rotational instability with severe functional impairment;
(14) Ankylosis, contracture deformity of the ankle joint, or loss of up to fifty percent of joint range of motion;
(15) Fracture of the femoral shaft complicated by pseudoarthrosis, malunion with shortening exceeding 5 cm, angular deformity exceeding 30 degrees, or severe rotational deformity;
(16) Nonunion of femoral neck fracture, necrosis of the femoral head, or malunion severely affecting lower limb function;
(17) Fracture of the tibia and fibula complicated by pseudoarthrosis, malunion with shortening exceeding 5 cm, angular deformity exceeding 30 degrees, or severe rotational deformity;
(18) Open or closed fracture of a long bone of a limb (humerus, radius, ulna, femur, tibia, fibula) complicated by chronic osteomyelitis;
(19) Cicatricial contracture of soft tissue of a limb affecting major joint movement, with loss of up to fifty percent of range of motion;
(20) Injury to an important nerve of a limb (brachial plexus and its important branches, lumbosacral plexus and its important branches) severely affecting limb motor function;
(21) Injury to an important blood vessel of a limb causing circulatory disturbance severely affecting limb function.

Chapter III Disfigurement of Appearance

Article 9 "Disfigurement of a person's appearance" means damaging a person's appearance [3], causing significant deformation, ugliness, or functional impairment.

Article 10 "Damage to the eye area" means any of the following circumstances:
(1) Loss or atrophy of one eyeball;
(2) Ptosis of either eyelid completely covering the pupil;
(3) Eyelid injury significantly affecting appearance;
(4) Injury to one eye area causing complete rupture of the nasolacrimal duct and rupture of the medial canthal ligament affecting appearance;
(5) Significant collapse of one orbital bone fracture.

Article 11 "Damage to the auricle" means any of the following circumstances:
(1) Loss of up to fifty percent of one auricle, or total loss area of both auricles exceeding sixty percent of one ear;
(2) Auricular injury causing significant deformation.

Article 12 "Defect, collapse, or distortion of the nose" causing significant deformation.

Article 13 Lip injury significantly affecting appearance.

Article 14 Zygomatic bone injury causing an opening degree (distance between incisal edges of upper and lower incisors) of less than 1.5 cm; malunion of zygomatic fracture causing significant deformation of appearance.

Article 15 Damage to the maxilla, mandible, and temporomandibular joint means any of the following circumstances:
(1) Fracture of the maxilla or mandible causing significant deformation of appearance;
(2) Loss or fracture of seven or more teeth in total;
(3) Injury to the temporomandibular joint causing an opening degree of less than 1.5 cm, or deviation of the mandible to the injured side causing significant asymmetry of the lower face.

Article 16 "Other disfigurement of appearance" means any of the following circumstances:
(1) Facial injury leaving obvious patchy scars, with a single scar area greater than 4 square centimeters, two scar areas greater than 7 square centimeters, total area of three or more scars greater than 9 square centimeters; or leaving obvious linear scars, with a single scar longer than 5 cm, cumulative length of two scars longer than 8 cm, cumulative total length of three or more scars longer than 10 cm, causing disfigurement of eyelids, nose, lips, cheeks, etc., or functional impairment.
(2) Facial nerve injury causing paralysis of most of the facial muscles on one side, resulting in incomplete eyelid closure and wry mouth;
(3) Facial injury leaving patchy fine scars, obvious pigmentation, or obvious depigmentation covering up to thirty percent of the facial area;
(4) Deep second-degree or higher burns or scalds to the face and neck resulting in cicatricial contracture significantly affecting appearance or severely impairing neck movement.

Chapter IV Loss of Hearing [4]

Article 17 After injury, hearing loss of one ear for speech sounds is above 91 decibels.

Article 18 After injury, hearing loss of both ears for speech sounds is above 60 decibels.

Chapter V Loss of Vision [5]

Article 19 "Loss of vision caused by various injuries" means any of the following circumstances:
(1) After injury, blindness in one eye;
(2) After injury, low vision in both eyes, with low vision of one eye being grade 2.

Article 20 Eye injury or craniocerebral injury causing visual field defect (visual field radius less than 10 degrees).

Chapter VI Loss of Function of Other Organs

Article 21 "Loss of function of other organs" means loss of function or severe impairment of function of organs other than hearing and vision. Where otherwise provided by provisions, those provisions shall apply.

Article 22 Diplopia (double vision) that cannot be restored after eye injury or craniocerebral injury, affecting work and life.

Article 23 Fracture of the maxilla or mandible, or injury to oral tissues or organs (e.g., tongue injury) causing significant impairment of speech, mastication, or swallowing ability.

Article 24 Loss of voice or severe hoarseness that cannot be restored after laryngeal injury.

Article 25 Scarring and stenosis of the pharynx or esophagus after injury causing dysphagia.

Article 26 Scarring and stenosis of the nasal cavity, pharynx, or larynx after injury causing dyspnea [6].

Article 27 Injury to both breasts of a female causing loss of lactation ability.

Article 28 Kidney injury complicated by renal hypertension, severe renal dysfunction.

Article 29 Ureteral injury leaving stricture causing hydronephrosis, severe renal dysfunction.

Article 30 Urethral injury leaving stricture causing dysuria, severe renal dysfunction.

Article 31 Anal canal injury causing severe fecal incontinence or severe anal stenosis.

Article 32 Pelvic fracture causing severe impairment of function of organs within the pelvic cavity.

Article 33 Uterine or adnexal injury in the later stage complicated by atrophy of internal genitalia or affecting development of internal genitalia.

Article 34 Vaginal injury involving surrounding organs causing fistula formation or scarring leading to severe functional impairment.

Article 35 Penile injury causing loss of the penis, severe deformity leading to severe functional impairment.

Article 36 Testicular or vas deferens injury causing loss of reproductive ability.

Chapter VII Other Serious Harm to Human Health

Article 37 "Other serious harm to human health" means, in addition to the serious injuries mentioned above, injuries that are life-threatening at the time of injury, or that may cause life-threatening complications during the course of the injury, as well as other injuries that seriously affect human health.

Section 1 Craniocerebral Injury

Article 38 Scalp avulsion covering up to twenty-five percent of the scalp area and accompanied by hemorrhagic shock; scalp injury causing loss of vitality of the scalp covering up to twenty-five percent of the scalp area.

Article 39 Skull fracture (e.g., linear, depressed, comminuted) accompanied by injury to brain parenchyma and blood vessels, with signs and symptoms of cerebral compression; rupture of the dura mater.

Article 40 Open craniocerebral injury.

Article 41 Skull base fracture accompanied by injury to the facial or auditory nerve, or long-term non-healing of cerebrospinal fluid leakage.

Article 42 Craniocerebral injury causing immediate coma (lasting more than 30 minutes) and neurological signs such as monoplegia, hemiplegia, aphasia, etc.

Article 43 Craniocerebral injury showing cerebral contusion on brain CT scan, but must be accompanied by neurological symptoms and signs.

Article 44 Craniocerebral injury causing epidural hematoma, subdural hematoma, or intracerebral hematoma.

Article 45 Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage accompanied by neurological symptoms and signs.

Article 46 Craniocerebral injury causing intracranial infection, such as meningitis, brain abscess, etc.

Article 47 Craniocerebral injury causing damage to cranial nerves other than the olfactory nerve that is difficult to recover.

Article 48 Craniocerebral injury causing traumatic epilepsy.

Article 49 Craniocerebral injury causing severe organic mental disorder.

Article 50 Symptoms and signs caused by substantial damage to the nervous system from craniocerebral injury, such as carotid-cavernous sinus fistula, hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction, etc.

Section 2 Neck Injury

Article 51 Injury to the throat, trachea, neck, floor of the mouth, or adjacent tissues causing dyspnea.

Article 52 Neck injury causing thrombosis of one carotid artery or vertebral artery, carotid-jugular fistula, or pseudoaneurysm.

Article 53 Neck injury involving the brachial plexus, severely affecting upper limb function; neck injury involving the apex of the pleura causing pneumothorax with dyspnea.

Article 54 Thyroid injury accompanied by recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causing severe functional impairment.

Article 55 Thoracic duct injury.

Article 56 Pharyngeal or esophageal injury causing local abscess, mediastinitis, or sepsis.

Article 57 Neck injury causing foreign body retention in the deep neck, affecting the function of corresponding tissues or organs.

Section 3 Chest Injury

Article 58 Chest injury causing hemothorax or pneumothorax, and causing dyspnea.

Article 59 Rib fracture causing dyspnea.

Article 60 Sternal fracture causing dyspnea.

Article 61 Chest injury causing mediastinal emphysema, respiratory distress syndrome, or rupture of the trachea or bronchus.

Article 62 Tracheal or esophageal injury causing mediastinitis, mediastinal abscess, mediastinal emphysema, hemopneumothorax, or empyema.

Article 63 Cardiac injury; injury to a major blood vessel of the chest.

Article 64 Chest injury causing empyema, lung abscess, atelectasis, bronchopleural fistula, esophagopleural fistula, or bronchoesophageal fistula.

Article 65 Severe compression of the chest causing circulatory disturbance, respiratory movement disturbance, or intracranial hemorrhage.

Article 66 Loss of one breast in a female.

Section 4 Abdominal Injury

Article 67 Perforation or rupture of the stomach, intestines, or biliary tract.

Article 68 Rupture of the liver, spleen, pancreas, or other organs; formation of hematoma or abscess in these organs due to injury.

Article 69 Renal rupture; urinary extravasation requiring surgical treatment (including renal artery embolization).

Article 70 Ureteral injury causing urinary extravasation.

Article 71 Abdominal injury causing peritonitis, sepsis, intestinal obstruction, or intestinal fistula, etc.

Article 72 Abdominal injury causing intra-abdominal hemorrhage requiring surgical treatment.

Section 5 Pelvic Injury

Article 73 Severe deformation of pelvic fracture.

Article 74 Urethral laceration or rupture requiring surgical repair.

Article 75 Bladder rupture.

Article 76 Scrotal avulsion covering up to fifty percent of scrotal skin area; loss of both testicles.

Article 77 Injury causing perforation or rupture of the uterus or adnexa.

Article 78 Injury to a pregnant woman causing premature birth, stillbirth, premature separation of the placenta, abortion complicated by hemorrhagic shock or severe infection.

Article 79 Severe injury to the vulva or vagina of a young girl.

Section 6 Spinal and Spinal Cord Injury

Article 80 Spinal fracture or dislocation accompanied by spinal cord injury or injury to multiple spinal nerves.

Article 81 Substantial damage to the spinal cord affecting spinal cord function, such as severe impairment of limb motor function, sexual function, or bowel and bladder control.

Section 7 Other Injuries

Article 82 Burns and scalds.
(1) Total area of burns or scalds in adults (excluding first-degree burns, the same below) is thirty percent or more, or third-degree burns are ten percent or more; total area in children is ten percent or more, or third-degree burns are five percent or more. Burns or scalds with an area less than the above but with any of the following circumstances:
1. Occurrence of shock;
2. Poisoning from inhalation of toxic gases;
3. Severe respiratory tract burns;
4. Accompanied by complications leading to serious consequences;
5. Other similar circumstances as above.
(2) Deep second-degree burns or scalds to special areas (such as face, hands, perineum, etc.) severely affecting appearance and function, with reference to the relevant provisions of these Standards.

Article 83 Frostbite causing necrosis of ears, nose, hands, feet, etc., and severe functional impairment, with reference to the relevant provisions of these Standards.

Article 84 Electric injury accompanied by severe complications or residual functional impairment, with reference to the relevant provisions of these Standards.

Article 85 Injury caused by physical, chemical, or biological factors causing severe functional impairment of organs, with reference to the relevant provisions of these Standards.

Article 86 Injury causing foreign body retention in important organs such as the brain, heart, or lungs.

Article 87 Injury causing traumatic shock, hemorrhagic shock, or septic shock.

Article 88 Subcutaneous hemorrhage covering up to thirty percent of the total body surface area; hemorrhage of muscles and deep tissues accompanied by complications or residual severe functional impairment.

Article 89 Injury causing fat embolism syndrome.

Article 90 Injury causing crush syndrome.

Article 91 Respiratory obstruction caused by various reasons, with signs of asphyxia and accompanied by complications or residual functional impairment.

Chapter VIII Supplementary Provisions

Article 92 For injuries that meet the requirements of Article 85 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China but are not specifically provided for in these Standards, an identification may be made by analogy with the corresponding provisions of these Standards.
The identification prescribed in the preceding paragraph shall be made or reviewed by a forensic medical identification institution at or above the prefecture (city) level.

Article 93 Where three or more injuries (or types of injuries) are each close to the standards of the relevant provisions of these Standards, a comprehensive assessment may be made to determine whether a serious injury exists, based on the specific circumstances.

Article 94 The terms "above" and "below" as used in these Standards include the number itself.

Article 95 These Standards apply only to the forensic medical identification of serious injuries as prescribed in the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China.

Article 96 These Standards shall come into effect as of July 1, 1990. The "Standards for Identification of Serious Injuries (for Trial Implementation)" issued in 1986 shall be simultaneously abolished.
Before the implementation of these Standards, where an identification has already been made but a judgment has not yet been rendered, the "Standards for Identification of Serious Injuries (for Trial Implementation)" issued in 1986 shall still apply.

March 29, 1990

Notes on the Standards for Identification of Serious Injuries

(1) When assessing joint range of motion, judgment shall be made based on the overall function of the examined joint, and comprehensive analysis may be performed with reference to the commonly used clinical normal human joint range of motion values. During examination, the past functional status of the joint must be understood and compared with the range of motion of the contralateral joint.

(2) "Opposition" refers to the action of the pulp of the thumb opposing the pulp of each of the other fingers.

(3) The facial area refers to the region below the anterior hairline, between the anterior borders of the two ears and the lower edge of the mandible, including the forehead, orbital region, nose, lips, chin, zygomatic region, cheeks, parotid-masseter region, and auricles.

(4) Methods for assessing hearing loss:
Hearing examination should preferably use a pure-tone audiometer with air conduction as the standard, with the hearing level unit being the decibel (dB). Generally, the average of three frequencies (500, 1000, and 2000 Hz) is used. This average corresponds to the hearing threshold for conversational speech.
Hearing loss below 25 dB is considered normal hearing.
After injury, hearing loss in both ears is calculated as follows:
(Hearing loss of the better ear x 5 + hearing loss of the poorer ear x 1) divided by 6. If the calculated result is hearing loss above 60 dB, it constitutes a serious injury.
Correction for presbycusis: starting from age 60, a decrement of 0.5 dB per year is applied.
For hearing examinations, when the identifier deems it necessary, appropriate methods (such as acoustic impedance, electrocochleography, auditory brainstem evoked potentials, etc.) may be selected for measurement.

(5) Methods for assessing visual impairment:
If the distance vision of the injured eye, without correction or with lenses (including contact lenses, pinhole lenses, etc.), can reach the normal vision range (0.8 or above) or near-normal vision range (0.4-0.8), it shall not be considered as visual impairment. If central vision is good but the visual field is narrowed, with a visual field radius of less than 10 degrees but greater than 5 degrees around the fixation point, it is grade 3; if the radius is less than 5 degrees, it is grade 4.
When assessing visual impairment, "distance vision" shall be the standard, with reference to "near vision".

(6) Dyspnea is assessed in accordance with the following standards:
(Content omitted as per original)

②Central vision examination method: Use a standard universal visual acuity chart to examine distance vision and near vision. For patients with craniocerebral injury, examination of central scotoma, physiological blind spot, and visual field shall be conducted. For those with diplopia, a more detailed examination shall be performed to analyze the nature and degree of the diplopia.

③Regarding vision examination, if the forensic expert deems it necessary, appropriate methods (such as visual electrophysiology) may be selected for testing.

(6) Dyspnea is caused by ventilatory demand exceeding the ventilatory capacity of the respiratory organs. Symptoms: subjective shortness of breath, feeling of insufficient air, chest tightness and discomfort. Signs: increased respiratory rate, increased or decreased depth of respiration, possibly accompanied by abnormal periodicity, nasal flaring, cyanosis, etc. Laboratory tests:

①Arterial blood gas analysis: arterial oxygen partial pressure may be below 8.0 KPa (60 mmHg);

②Chest X-ray examination;

③Pulmonary function test.

Diagnosis of dyspnea must be accompanied by both symptoms and signs. Laboratory tests are for reference.
